# Reshaping data: `tidyr`

## Why tidy? {.smaller}

![](figs/01_tidy-data.png){fig-alt="Same data table shown three times: columns marked as variables, rows marked as observations, and individual cells marked as values." height=3in fig-align=center}

- **Consistency**: If there is a consistent data structure, it’s easier to learn the tools that work with that structure due to the underlying uniformity.
- **Vectorization**: R and the tidyverse are built to operate on columns of values, allowing R's vectorization to shine.
  - A tidy layout is a natural byproduct.

## Same data, three layouts {.smaller}
These three tables all describe tuberculosis (TB) surveillance: country, year, number of cases, and population.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r table1}

table1

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r table2}

table2

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r table3}

table3

```
:::

::::

- `table1` matches the format on the prior slide. Each column is a variable and each row is an observation per country per year. Each cell is a value.

## Tidy data in action {.smaller}

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

1. Computing a rate.

```{r tidy-ex1}

table1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(rate = cases / population * 10000)

```
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

2. Calculating totals by year.

```{r tidy-ex2}

table1 |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarize(total_cases = sum(cases))

```
:::

::::

3. Plotting.

```{r tidy-ex3}
#| output-location: "column"
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6

table1 |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = year, y = cases)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(aes(group = country)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(aes(color = country, 
                          shape = country)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1999, 2000))

```

Try writing code using `table2` or `table3` instead (it takes a lot more work).

## Data reshaping with `pivot_*`
:::notes
- These reorganize values into a new layout.
:::

- The two main functions to reshape and tidy data are `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`.
- **"Lengthen"** data by collapsing several columns into two.
- **"Widen"** data by expanding two columns into several.

## Lengthening data: Glucose data {.smaller}
::: notes
- Long format will make it easier to plot trajectories over time
- Calculate averages per subject or per day
:::

A diabetes-prevention study asks six participants to record fasting glucose (mg/dL) each morning for six days. Some participants' monitors stopped recording early and are recorded as `NA`.

```{r glucose-wide}

glucose_wide = tibble::tribble( # create a tbl and fill by row
  ~patient_id, ~day1, ~day2, ~day3, ~day4, ~day5, ~day6, # defines column names
  "P001",        132,   128,   119,   141,    NA,    NA,
  "P002",         98,   101,   105,    99,   103,   107,
  "P003",        210,   195,   188,    NA,    NA,    NA,
  "P004",        145,   150,   142,   138,   130,    NA,
  "P005",         88,    91,    85,    90,    92,    89,
  "P006",        175,   168,    NA,    NA,    NA,    NA
)
glucose_wide

```

. . .

- This data is in "wide" format: there is one observation per person.
- We would like to *reshape* the data such that each row represents one glucose reading per day per patient.
  - The column names (`day1` ... `day6`) will be *values* of a variable, not variable names.

## How `pivot_longer` works {.smaller}
:::notes
- Column names (`bp1`, `bp2`) become values in the new `measurement` column, repeated once per original row
- Cell values get unwound row by row into the new `value` column
:::

![](figs/02a_pivot-wider-names.png){fig-alt="Wide-to-long reshaping diagram, colored to highlight that the bp1 and bp2 column names become values in the new 'measurement' column." height=2.5in fig-align=center}

![](figs/02b_pivot-wider-values.png){fig-alt="Same wide-to-long reshaping diagram, but now colored to highlight that the cell values from the bp1 and bp2 columns become entries in the new 'value' column." height=2.5in fig-align=center}

`pivot_wider()` is just the opposite direction!

## `pivot_longer()` {.smaller}

```{r pivot-longer1}

glucose_wide |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = day1:day6, # columns to pivot
    names_to = "day", # single column name for old names
    values_to = "glucose" # column name for values
  )

```

Let's breakdown the arguments of the function:

- `cols`: which columns to pivot (same syntax as `dplyr::select()`).
- `names_to`: name for the new column that holds the old column *names*.
- `values_to`: name for the new column that holds the cell *values*.
- `"day"` and `"glucose"` are quoted because they are new variables that don't exist yet.

## `pivot_longer()`: Alternative syntax {.smaller}
::: notes
- Could tell R which columns to drop instead of keep
- Could tell R to use regex
:::

```{r pivot-longer2}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| output-location: "column"

glucose_wide |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = !patient_id,
    names_to = "day",
    values_to = "glucose"
  )

```

```{r pivot-longer3}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| output-location: "column"

glucose_wide |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = tidyselect::starts_with("day"),
    names_to = "day", # single column name for old names
    values_to = "glucose" # column name for values
  )

```

## Regex: The `day` variable {.smaller}
- We don't really need the `day` prefix for the values in the `day` variable.
- `parse_number()` is a [function](https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/parse_number.html) that drops any non-numeric characters before the first number and all characters after the first number.
  - Example of regular expressions (project idea!!)

. . .

```{r longer-regex}

glucose.long = glucose_wide |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = day1:day6,
    names_to = "day",
    values_to = "glucose"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(day = readr::parse_number(day))

glucose.long

```

## Plotting long data {.smaller}
::: notes
This would have been significantly harder without tidying our data
:::

```{r longer-plot}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| warning: TRUE

glucose.long |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = day, y = glucose, color = patient_id)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

```

- Note: `ggplot2` automatically dropped the `NA` values for us and provided a warning.

## Widening Data: Patient survey data {.smaller}
- Increasing the number of columns (reducing the number of rows), by spreading one observation across columns.

```{r cms-data}

cms_patient_experience

```

- Centers for Medicare \& Medicaid Services data:
  - One row per measure, six measures per organization.
  - Want to look at measures per organization $\rightarrow$ one row per organization.


## Patient survey data: Measures {.smaller}

```{r cms-data-distinct}

cms_patient_experience |>
  dplyr::distinct(measure_cd, measure_title)

```

- `measure_title` gives a description of the measure coded in `measure_cd`. We'll focus on the latter for now since it is shorter and better for naming.

. . .

- `pivot_wider()` has the opposite interface to pivot_longer(). 
  - Instead of choosing new column names, we need to provide the existing columns that define the values (`values_from`) and the column name (`names_from`).
  - E.g., `names_from = measure_cd`.


## `pivot_wider()` {.smaller}
Now let's apply these principals to the `cms_patient_experience` data.

```{r cms-wide1}

cms_patient_experience |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = org_pac_id:org_nm,
    names_from = measure_cd,
    values_from = prf_rate
  )

```

. . . 

- Both `org_pac_id` and `org_nm` uniquely determine the organization and should be used as the `id_cols` input.
- Notice `measure_title` was dropped since we did not include it in `id_cols`, `names_from`, or `values_from`.

## Reshaping summary {.smaller}
- Tidy data:
  - Variables in columns.
  - Observations in rows.
  - One value per cell. 
- `pivot_longer()`: columns $\rightarrow$ rows.
  - Use when column names are values, not variable names.
- `pivot_wider()`: rows $\rightarrow$ columns.
  - Use when one observation is spread across multiple rows.
- Both functions **preserve information**, only reshaping the data frame.

# Importing data: `readr`

## Reading data from a file {.smaller}
::: notes
- Notice the hard coded NA values this will be important later
:::

- The `patients.csv` file in the `data` folder is a type of file with **c**omma-**s**eparated **v**alues.
  - On your computer you can open it with Excel but is is different from a .xlsx file, which support rich formatting, charts, equations, and multiple sheets.
- Alternatively, .csv files can always be open with a plain-text editor (e.g., TextEdit or Notepad).
  - If we do so, our data looks like:
  
```
Patient ID,First Name,diagnosis.code,treatmentGroup,AGE
1,Alicia,Asthma,Inhaled corticosteroid,4
2,Ben,Eczema,Topical steroid,5
3,Carla,N/A,N/A,7
4,Diego,Allergic rhinitis,Antihistamine,
5,Priya,Asthma,Inhaled corticosteroid,five
6,Owen,Eczema,Topical steroid,6
```

- The `readr` [package](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) provide a fast and friendly way to read rectangular data from delimited files.
  - Including comma-separated values (CSV) and tab-separated values (TSV) files.

## `read_csv()` {.smaller}
- The `patients.csv` sits in the `data` folder of our directory. Since we use R projects, our working directory is already the root directory where our `.Rproj` sits.
  - For you this is your `PUBHLT0411` folder.
- This way, when we read in any data, we only need to specify the path after this (relative path).
  - For me, I set a single data folder in the root directory $\rightarrow$ `data/module05/patients.csv`.
- Macs use `/` in paths and Windows use `\`.

. . .

```{r patients-data1}
#| message: TRUE

patients = readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/patients.csv")) # relative path

```

- `readr` reports the number of rows/columns, the delimiter, and its guess at each column's type.

## `here` {.smaller}
- Notice that we when we read in our file with `readr::read_csv`, we wrapped our `file = ` argument in the `here::here()` function.
- The goal of the `here` [package](https://here.r-lib.org/) is to is to enable easy file referencing in project-oriented workflows.
  - It creates paths relative to where your .Rproj sits.
- E.g., `here::here("data/module05/patients.csv")` creates `"/Users/rdeek/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofPittsburgh/Documents/teaching/PUBHLT0411/data/module05/patients.csv"` for me.

. . .

- This is **not** needed for reading files into R when using an .Rproj, as the working directory will already be set to the path where your project sits.

. . .

- But it **is** needed when knitting a document because knitr automatically changes the working directory to the folder containing the .rmd/.qmd file.

## `read_csv()` and missing data {.smaller}
:::notes
- Go to previous slide and see NA for age is an actual blank whereas N/A is written for diagnosis.
- By default blanks "" are the read as NA need to tell R other codings
:::

```{r patients-data2}

patients

```

- Notice there are two types of `NA` values: `N/A` and `<NA>`. The latter of the two is coded correctly.

. . .

```{r patients-data3}

patients = readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/patients.csv"), na = c("N/A", ""))
patients

```

- The `na` argument can be used to specify several different missing-value designations at once.

## Transform imported data {.smaller}
- `Patient ID` and `Full Name` contain spaces, which we know doesn't constitute a machine readable name.

```{r patients-data4}

patients |>
  dplyr::rename(
    patient_id = `Patient ID`,
    first_name  = `First Name`
  )

```

- The space requires the use of backticks to refer to the variable.

## `rename()` vs. `janitor` package
- When many (potentially most, if not all) names have a messy structure using `janitor::clean_names()` is a better option than renaming all variables individually.

```{r patients-data5}

patients |> janitor::clean_names()

```

- Converts every column name to `snake_case` in one step.
  - Handles the spaces, the period in `diagnosis.code`, the camelCase `treatmentGroup`, and caps in `AGE`.

## Transform imported data {.smaller}
`treatment_group` has a fixed, known set of values, meaning it can be coded as a factor, instead of plain string.

```{r patients-data6}

patients |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  dplyr::mutate(treatment_group = factor(treatment_group))

```

. . .

Patient 5's age was entered as `"five"`, so the `age` column was read in as string/character.

```{r patients_clean7}

patients_clean = patients |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    treatment_group = factor(treatment_group),
    age = as.numeric(ifelse(age == "five", "5", age)) # as.numeric to convert chr -> dbl
  )
patients_clean

```

## Other file types
`readr` has a function for many format types:

- `read_csv2()`: semicolon-delimited
- `read_tsv()`: tab-delimited
- `read_delim()`: any delimiter, guessed automatically if you don't specify one
- `read_fwf()`: fixed-width columns
- `read_table()`: whitespace-separated fixed-width columns
- `read_log()`: Apache-style log files

Notice that there is no `read_*` function for .xlsx files. You'll need the `readxl` package for this.

## How readr guesses types
- A CSV file doesn’t contain any information about the type of each variable, so `readr` guesses the type.
  - Only `T` / `F` / `TRUE` / `FALSE`? $\rightarrow$ logical
  - Only numbers? $\rightarrow$ numeric
  - Matches the ISO8601 standard? $\rightarrow$ date / date-time
  - Otherwise $\rightarrow$ string

```{r readr-guess-type1}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/glucose_types_demo.csv"))
```

## Problems with guessing types
- Most data sets aren't tidy and there will be many incorrect guesses. Imagine a missing numeric value code as `.` instead of leaving it blank:

```{r readr-guess-type2}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/sbp_missing.csv"))
```

The entire vector (column) was forced to a character because of the `.`.

## Specifying column types {.smaller}
- `col_types` takes a named list where the names match the column names in the CSV file.

```{r readr-define-type1}
#| warning: TRUE 

sbp = readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/sbp_missing.csv"), 
                      col_types = list(sbp = col_double()) )
readr::problems(sbp)
sbp

```

. . .

- **Types:** `col_logical()`, `col_double()`, `col_integer()`, `col_character()`, `col_factor()`, `col_date()`, `col_datetime()`.

## Writing data
- Just as we can read files, we can export files with `write_*`.

```r
readr::write_csv(x = patients_clean, file = here::here("data/module05/patients-clean.csv"))
```

- If we were to import the exported dataset, `readr` start from scratch (e.g., guess the columns again, with no knowledge of the work we previously did).

. . .

- `.rds` is R’s custom binary format. When you you reload the object, you are loading the **exact same** R object that you stored
  - `read_rds` and `write_rds`.

```r
readr::write_rds(x = patients_clean, file = here::here("patients-clean.rds"))
```

# Joining data: `dplyr`

## Joining datasets
- Sometimes you will have many data frames that need to be joined together to perform the appropriate analysis.
- **Mutating joins** add new variables to one data frame from matching observations in another.

![](figs/03_join-dfs.png){fig-alt="Diagram of two tables, x and y, with color-coded matching and non-matching key values (1, 2 match; 3 and 4 are unique to each table)." height=3in fig-align=center}

::: aside
From: [https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/)
:::

## Left join

![](figs/04_left-join.gif){fig-alt="Animation of left_join(x, y): all rows from x are kept (keys 1, 2, 3), with matching y values joined in; key 4 from y is dropped." height=3in fig-align=center}

> All rows from `x`, and all columns from `x` and `y`. Rows in `x` with no match in `y` will have `NA` values in the new columns from `y`.

::: aside
From: [https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/)
:::

## Right join

![](figs/05_right-join.gif){fig-alt="Animation of right_join(x, y): all rows from y are kept (keys 1, 2, 4), with matching x values joined in; key 3 from x is dropped." height=3in fig-align=center}

> All rows from `y`, and all columns from `x` and `y`. Rows in `y` with no match in `x` will have `NA` values in the new columns from `x`.

::: aside
From: [https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/)
:::

## Full join

![](figs/06_full-join.gif){fig-alt="Animation of full_join(x, y): all rows from both x and y are kept (keys 1, 2, 3, 4), with NA filled in where no match exists." height=3in fig-align=center}

> All rows and all columns from both `x` and `y`. Where there are no matching values, returns `NA` for the one missing.

::: aside
From: [https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/)
:::

## Inner join

![](figs/07_inner-join.gif){fig-alt="Animation of inner_join(x, y): only rows with matching keys in both x and y are kept (keys 1 and 2); keys 3 and 4 are dropped." height=3in fig-align=center}

> All rows from `x` where there are matching values in `y`, and all columns from `x` and `y`.

::: aside
From: [https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/](https://www.garrickadenbuie.com/project/tidyexplain/)
:::

## Join `by`
- The default in the `join_*` functions is to join based on matching column names between the two data frames.
  - Alternatively, the column name can be specified explicity using `by = dplyr::join_by(col_name)`.
- When the column names for the unique identifier is different between the two data sets use `by = join_by(colname_in_x == colname_in_y)`.

## Joining with metadata and labs {.smaller}

```{r echo = F}

metadata = readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/metadata.csv"))
labdata = readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/labs.csv"))

```

```{r joins1}
#| output-location: "column"

metadata

```

```{r joins2}
#| output-location: "column"

labdata

```

```{r joins3}

dplyr::inner_join(x = labdata, y = metadata, by = dplyr::join_by(patient_id))

```

# Appendix {visibility="uncounted"}

## Column names: Many variables {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- One challenging type of data tidying occurs when multiple pieces of information are stored in the column names.
- Would like to store these in separate new variables.

. . .

```{r who-data}

who2

```

- WHO tuberculosis diagnosis data: `country`, `year`, and 56 other columns like `sp_m_014`.
  - Contain the diagnosis method, sex, and age range in the column name.
  - E.g., `sp` = positive pulmonary smear, `m` = male, `014` = 0-14 year old.

## Column names: Many variables {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

```{r who-long}

who2 |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = !(country:year),
    names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"), 
    names_sep = "_", 
    values_to = "count" # column name for values
  )

```

- `names_to`: can take a *vector* of new column names.
- `names_sep`: tells `pivot_longer()` how to split each original column name into multiple *values*.

## Column names: Variables and values {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- Another challenging type of data tidying occurs when column names include a mix of variable values and variable names

```{r clinic-data}

clinic_visits = tibble::tribble(
  ~patient_id, ~date_visit1,  ~sbp_visit1, ~date_visit2,  ~sbp_visit2,
  1,           "2023-01-05",  128,         "2023-04-02",  122,
  2,           "2023-01-06",  145,         NA,            NA,
  3,           "2023-01-10",  118,         "2023-04-15",  115,
  4,           "2023-01-12",  160,         "2023-04-20",  150,
  5,           "2023-01-15",  135,         NA,            NA
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(tidyselect::starts_with("date"), as.Date))

clinic_visits

```

- The column names of this dataset contain the names of two variables (`date`, `sbp`) and the values of another (`visit`, with values 1 or 2)

## `pivot_longer`: The `.value` sentinel {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- A vector must be supplied to `names_to` but this time we use the special "`.value`" sentinel.
  - This isn’t the name of a variable but a unique value that tells `pivot_longer()` to override the usual `values_to` argument.

```{r clinic-data-long1}
#| output-location: "column"

clinic_visits |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = !patient_id,
    names_to = c(".value", "visit"),
    names_sep = "_visit"
  )

```

- Uses the first component of the pivoted column names (`date`, `sbp`) as a variable name in the output.
- Could use `values_drop_na = TRUE` to remove the rows for the second visit that never happened.


##  How `pivot_wider()` works {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
Let's use a simple dataset of blood pressure measurements to illustrate how `pivot_wider()` works.

```{r bp-data}

bp.df = tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~measurement, ~value,
  "A",        "bp1",    100,
  "B",        "bp1",    140,
  "B",        "bp2",    115,
  "A",        "bp2",    120,
  "A",        "bp3",    105
)
bp.df
```

. . .

```{r bp-data-wide}

bp.df |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = measurement,
    values_from = value
  )

```

##  How `pivot_wider()` works {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
1. New **column names** are unique values of the `names_from = measurement` column.

```{r bp-data-step1}

bp.df |> 
  dplyr::distinct(measurement) |> 
  dplyr::pull()

```

. . .

2. New **rows** are unique combinations of everything else (the `id_cols`). Defaults to `id` data since there are only 3 columns.

```{r bp-data-step2}

bp.df |> 
  dplyr::select(!measurement & !value) |> # drop names_from and values_from columns
  dplyr::distinct()

```

. . .

3. Build an empty grid of `NA`s (then fills in values from the `values_from` input).

```{r bp-data-step3}

bp.df |> 
  dplyr::select(!measurement & !value) |> 
  dplyr::distinct() |> 
  dplyr::mutate(bp1 = NA, bp2 = NA, bp3 = NA)

```



## Troubleshooting in data tidying {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- It's plausible to imagine that one participant has two blood pressure readings on the same day.
  - What happens if their `id` and `measurement` variable is coded identically?
- It is also plausible that human error may create two observations with the same `id` and `measurement` values.

```{r bp-data-dup1}

bp.df.dup = tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~measurement, ~value,
  "A",        "bp1",    100,
  "A",        "bp1",    102,
  "A",        "bp2",    120,
  "B",        "bp1",    140,
  "B",        "bp2",    115
)

```

What would happen if we try to `pivot_wider` such data?

## Troubleshooting in data tidying {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
:::notes
- tidyr gives use the code to run to find duplicates
- We know which observations are causing the issue but imagine a dataset with hundreds, thousands, or millions of observations.
:::

`tidyr` warns that values aren't uniquely identified and return list-columns instead of plain numbers.

```{r bp-data-dup2}
#| warning: TRUE

bp.df.dup |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = measurement,
    values_from = value
  )

```

. . .

Trying the helper code:

```{r bp-data-dup3}

bp.df.dup |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(id, measurement)) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 1L)

```


## `read_csv()`: Skipping metadata rows {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- Typically, `read_csv` reads the first line of the data as the column names.
- It is not uncommon for a few lines of metadata to be included at the top of the file.
  - For example in `data/module05/clinic_report.csv`:

```
Community Health Screening Report
Site: Pittsburgh Public Health Clinic
patient_id,temp_c,heart_rate
1,37.2,78
2,38.9,102
3,36.8,65
```

. . .

```{r readr-skip1}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/clinic_report.csv"))
```

. . .

- The `skip` argument can help automatically remove these rows.

```{r readr-skip2}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/clinic_report.csv"), skip = 2)
```


## `read_csv()`: Skipping comment lines {visibility="uncounted"}
- Alternatively, sometimes comments are ended with a leading `#`.
  - For example in `data/module05/vitals_comment.csv`:

```
# Vitals collected during morning rounds, Ward B
patient_id,temp_c,heart_rate
1,37.2,78
2,38.9,102
3,36.8,65
```

- These lines can be skipped with the `comment` argument (or `skip`).

```{r readr-comments}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/vitals_comment.csv"), comment = "#")
```


## `read_csv()`: Files with no header row {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}
- Conversely, some data fils do not contain column names.
  - For example in `data/module05/vitals_nonames.csv`:

```
1,37.2,78
2,38.9,102
3,36.8,65
```

- Since `readr` assumes the first row are the column names we'll have to prevent this with the `col_names` argument.

```{r readr-colnames1}
readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/vitals_nonames.csv"), col_names = FALSE)
```

. . .

- Or pass in our own names.

```{r readr-colnames2}

readr::read_csv(file = here::here("data/module05/vitals_nonames.csv"),
                col_names = c("patient_id", "temp_c", "heart_rate") )

```
